treatmentPlan.firstLine: Mesalamine (5-ASA) or Sulfasalazine — anti-inflammatory, topical effect on colonic mucosa
treatmentPlan.timeline: Improvement within 1 week. Clinical remission may require 4-6 weeks or longer.
treatmentPlan.acuteExacerbation: Corticosteroids (prednisolone) in conjunction with 5-ASA during flares
treatmentPlan.maintenance: GI follow-up, surveillance colonoscopy (UC increases CRC risk)

pathophysiology.mechanism: Chronic relapsing inflammatory disorder limited to colonic mucosa and submucosa. Begins in rectum, extends proximally in continuous fashion. Neutrophils infiltrate crypts → crypt abscesses → crypt destruction → mucosal ulceration → bleeding (hematochezia). Unlike Crohn's: no transmural inflammation, no skip lesions, no granulomas, no small bowel involvement, rectum always involved.
pathophysiology.smokingNote: UC is more common in non-smokers and ex-smokers. Smoking is protective in UC (opposite of Crohn's). However, smoking cessation can trigger UC onset.
pathophysiology.colorectalCancer: UC increases CRC risk. Risk begins ~8-10 years after diagnosis. Surveillance colonoscopy required.

teachingPoints: Infection must be excluded before scope. Stool studies are the safety gate.
Abdominal XR is a quick screen before colonoscopy for gross pathology.
5-ASA (mesalamine) is first-line — topical anti-inflammatory. Steroids are for acute flares only.
Preventive care (vaccines) should be ordered at end of case, not before treatment.
GI consult is proper medical care even though it doesn't change the CCS score.
UC affects mucosa/submucosa only (no transmural). Rectum always involved. Continuous, not patchy.
